title: FTX: Where $8 Billion Went
note: FTX — full style: animated metaphors, varied doodles, real photos, mascot ~16%.

scenes.narration: In 2022, this was the most trusted man in crypto.
scenes.caption: The most trusted man in crypto
scenes.label: SBF

scenes.narration: Sam Bankman-Fried. Thirty years old, running FTX — one of the biggest crypto exchanges on Earth.
scenes.caption: FTX — a crypto giant

scenes.narration: At its peak, FTX was valued at thirty-two billion dollars. Sam himself was worth around twenty-six.
And he looked nothing like a villain. Messy hair, cargo shorts, slept on a beanbag, played video games in meetings.
scenes.caption: …not your typical tycoon

scenes.narration: He said he was only getting rich to give it all away. Effective altruism. The good billionaire.
scenes.caption: "the good billionaire"

scenes.narration: It wasn't just an image — he built a whole philanthropic brand around it.
He testified to Congress. Bailed out other crypto firms. People called him the J.P. Morgan of crypto.
scenes.caption: crypto's hero

scenes.narration: And then, in about ten days, all of it came crashing down.
scenes.caption: …to the ground

scenes.narration: Eight billion dollars of customer money — just gone.
So where did eight billion dollars of other people's money actually go?
Let's follow eight billion dollars — right out the back door.
scenes.heading: Where $8 Billion of Customer Money Went
scenes.sub: It didn't vanish. It was gambled.

scenes.narration: Crypto itself was on a rocket. Prices only went up, and everyone was sure this time was different.
scenes.caption: crypto: to the moon

scenes.narration: FTX put its name on a twenty-thousand-seat NBA arena, and hired A-list celebrities to sell it to you.
scenes.caption: the FTX Arena · a Super Bowl ad

scenes.narration: It gave tens of millions to politicians, becoming one of the biggest donors in the country.
The smartest venture funds on Earth lined up to invest, barely checking the books.
scenes.caption: top VCs piled in

scenes.narration: Millions of ordinary people trusted FTX with their savings. It felt as safe as a bank.
scenes.caption: millions trusted it

scenes.narration: Every signal said: this is the responsible one. The grown-up in a reckless industry.
scenes.caption: "the safe one"

scenes.narration: Which is exactly why what was happening underneath is so unsettling.
Remember the backdrop. In 2021, crypto was a mania. Prices doubled, tripled, and 'number go up' felt like a law of physics.
scenes.caption: 2021: the mania

scenes.narration: New coins launched every day. Teenagers became millionaires on paper. Nobody wanted to be the one asking boring questions.
scenes.caption: …everyone was getting rich

scenes.narration: In a gold rush, the calm, trusted figure selling the shovels looks like the safest bet of all.
scenes.caption: FTX sold the shovels

scenes.narration: And crypto's whole promise was to cut out the middlemen you have to trust — banks, brokers, gatekeepers.
The deep irony? FTX asked you to trust it completely — to be the exact middleman crypto was invented to avoid.
scenes.caption: …the middleman crypto was meant to kill

scenes.narration: To understand it, you need two companies. First, FTX. A crypto exchange.
scenes.caption: Company 1: FTX

scenes.narration: You send it your money, it lets you buy and sell crypto. Simple. Like a bank, but for coins.
scenes.caption: you deposit → you trade

scenes.narration: Second company: Alameda Research. A trading firm, making risky bets with its own money.
scenes.caption: Company 2: Alameda

scenes.narration: Both were quietly controlled by the same man. And Alameda was run by Caroline Ellison — Sam's on-and-off girlfriend.
scenes.caption: …both his
scenes.label: ONE BOSS

scenes.narration: Now, the single most sacred rule of running an exchange: customer money is untouchable. You never, ever gamble with it.
scenes.caption: rule #1: NEVER touch customer funds

scenes.narration: FTX touched it. Secretly, it funneled billions in customer deposits straight into Alameda.
scenes.caption: customer funds → Alameda

scenes.narration: There was literally a backdoor in the code — a secret setting that let Alameda borrow unlimited customer money, invisibly.
scenes.title: The backdoor

scenes.narration: And Alameda spent it. Risky bets. Venture investments. Mansions in the Bahamas. Political donations. Loans to the founders themselves.
scenes.caption: …your money, their lifestyle

scenes.narration: By the end, Alameda owed FTX's customers around eight billion dollars it did not have.
Think about what that means. When a normal exchange holds your money, it's supposed to just sit there, like cash in a safe-deposit box.
scenes.caption: your money should just… sit there

scenes.narration: You can take it out whenever you want, because it never moved. That's the entire promise.
scenes.caption: …always there when you want it

scenes.narration: FTX broke that promise in secret. Your deposit didn't sit in a vault. It was wired to the gambling desk next door.
scenes.caption: …instead it went to the casino

scenes.narration: And Alameda wasn't betting carefully. It was making huge, leveraged, often terrible bets.
scenes.caption: …huge, reckless bets

scenes.narration: When those bets lost, there was no safety net. Just a growing hole where the customer money used to be.
scenes.caption: …a growing hole

scenes.narration: This wasn't a grey area. Prosecutors would later call it exactly what it was — fraud, on a massive scale.
The founders even took personal loans — hundreds of millions — from the very funds their customers had deposited.
scenes.caption: …loans to themselves

scenes.narration: A real exchange keeps your money in a separate account it cannot spend. It's a basic, legally-required wall.
scenes.caption: the rule: a wall between the two

scenes.narration: FTX quietly knocked that wall down — and let the money pour through to Alameda.
scenes.caption: …the wall came down

scenes.narration: There was even a special exemption in the code so Alameda's account could go billions into the red without ever being shut off.
scenes.caption: …a secret 'never shut off' setting

scenes.narration: Everyone else playing on FTX would be auto-liquidated in seconds. Alameda alone could lose forever, on your dime.
scenes.caption: one set of rules for Alameda

scenes.narration: You might ask: how did nobody catch this? Simple. FTX had no proper auditor, no real board, and almost no oversight.
scenes.caption: no auditor · no board

scenes.narration: The people who were supposed to check the books were, essentially, Sam and his roommates.
scenes.caption: …the 'checkers' were his friends

scenes.narration: So the deposits flowed one way — out of your account, into the bets — and nobody with power ever said stop.
scenes.caption: …and nobody said stop

scenes.narration: For a while, it worked perfectly. The bets were winning, crypto was booming, and no one asked for all their money at once.
scenes.caption: …while the music played

scenes.narration: A machine like that only has to survive one thing: the day everybody wants out together.
scenes.caption: …until everyone wants out

scenes.narration: But here's the Enron-style trick that held it all together. FTX printed its own money.
scenes.caption: FTX invents a coin: FTT

scenes.narration: A token called FTT. FTX created it out of thin air, and it was worth whatever the market said — which FTX could nudge.
scenes.caption: FTT — conjured from nothing

scenes.narration: Now watch the loop. Alameda held billions in FTT as 'collateral.' So the whole empire was propped up by a coin its own sister company invented.
scenes.title: The circular trick

scenes.narration: It's the oldest magic trick in finance. Invent an asset, call it collateral, borrow real money against your own made-up coin.
scenes.caption: collateral… from nothing

scenes.narration: As long as FTT held its value, the machine kept spinning. It looked like a tower of gold. It was a tower of FTT.
scenes.caption: a tower of its own token

scenes.narration: Imagine a casino that pays its debts using chips it prints itself. As long as nobody cashes out, it looks infinitely rich.
scenes.caption: a casino paying with its own chips

scenes.narration: But those chips are only worth something because everyone agrees they are. Agreement is a very fragile kind of collateral.
scenes.caption: …value by agreement only

scenes.narration: If people ever doubt the chip, its price falls, and suddenly the 'collateral' propping everything up is worth almost nothing.
scenes.caption: doubt → the collateral vanishes

scenes.narration: FTX and Alameda were now bound together by this coin. If one fell, both fell.
scenes.caption: …tied together by FTT

scenes.narration: And every tower built on one block has the same flaw. Pull that block, and it all comes down.
scenes.caption: …one block holds it up

scenes.narration: On November second, a news site, CoinDesk, leaked Alameda's balance sheet. It was mostly FTT — its own partner's invented coin.
Then a rival stepped in. Changpeng Zhao — 'CZ' — the founder of Binance, the biggest exchange of all.
scenes.caption: CZ — founder of Binance
scenes.label: THE RIVAL

scenes.narration: On November sixth, CZ tweeted that Binance would dump its entire pile of FTT. One tweet.
scenes.caption: "we're selling our FTT"

scenes.narration: FTT crashed. And the instant it did, Alameda's collateral evaporated into nothing.
scenes.caption: FTT → worthless

scenes.narration: The tower came down.
scenes.caption: the FTT tower falls

scenes.narration: Suddenly the balance sheet everyone trusted was mostly a coin that was now in free-fall.
scenes.caption: …the 'assets' were evaporating

scenes.narration: Alameda couldn't repay. FTX couldn't cover it. The eight-billion-dollar hole was finally visible to everyone.
scenes.caption: …the hole, exposed

scenes.narration: And every customer had the same thought at the same second. Get my money out. Now.
scenes.caption: …get my money OUT

scenes.narration: A bank run is the one thing no exchange can survive if the money isn't really there. And FTX's money wasn't.
scenes.caption: the one thing it couldn't survive

scenes.narration: It became the fastest bank run in modern history.
scenes.caption: the run on FTX

scenes.narration: As it unraveled, Sam went on posting that everything was fine. 'FTX is fine. Assets are fine.' They were not.
scenes.caption: "FTX is fine." (it wasn't)

scenes.narration: For a few hours, CZ's Binance offered to swoop in and buy FTX — to save it.
scenes.caption: a rescue offer…

scenes.narration: Then Binance looked at the books, saw the size of the hole, and walked away within a day.
Because there was nothing to rescue. The customer money that should have been there simply wasn't.
scenes.caption: …nothing left to save

scenes.narration: Five billion dollars of withdrawals in seventy-two hours. FTX couldn't pay — the money was gone, gambled away at Alameda.
From leak to bankruptcy took nine days.
scenes.title: November 2022

scenes.narration: On November eleventh, FTX filed for bankruptcy. Eight billion dollars — gone.
scenes.caption: …$8 billion

scenes.narration: And the damage didn't stop at FTX. Its collapse knocked over other crypto firms like dominoes.
scenes.caption: …the contagion spread

scenes.narration: People called it crypto's Lehman moment. The trust that held the whole industry together cracked overnight.
scenes.caption: crypto's "Lehman moment"

scenes.narration: On the way down, hundreds of millions more mysteriously drained out in a hack nobody has fully explained.
scenes.caption: …and then it got hacked

scenes.narration: The man brought in to clean up the wreckage was John Ray — the same expert who untangled Enron.
scenes.caption: the cleanup expert: John Ray

scenes.narration: His verdict was damning: in forty years, he'd never seen such a complete failure of corporate controls.
No proper books. No board. Company funds tracked on casual group chats. A thirty-billion-dollar company run like a dorm room.
scenes.caption: …run like a dorm room

scenes.narration: So when the withdrawals hit, there was nothing underneath. The whole thing came down in a single week.
scenes.caption: nothing underneath

scenes.narration: Thirty billion dollars of value, gone — faster than it takes most people to notice their bank app updated.
scenes.caption: $30B → zero in a week

scenes.narration: Sam was arrested in the Bahamas, and extradited to New York to face trial.
scenes.caption: arrested in the Bahamas
scenes.label: UNDER ARREST

scenes.narration: And one by one, his inner circle turned on him. Caroline Ellison, Gary Wang, Nishad Singh — all pleaded guilty and testified.
scenes.caption: his inner circle flips

scenes.narration: The same genius-founder the magazines had put on their covers was now defendant number one.
His own ex-girlfriend, who ran Alameda, became the star witness against him.
In November 2023, a jury found him guilty on all seven counts.
Sam Bankman-Fried was sentenced to twenty-five years in prison.
The judge said plainly what had happened: he stole about eight billion dollars from FTX's customers.
The good billionaire, the effective altruist, the J.P. Morgan of crypto — was running the biggest fraud since Enron.
scenes.caption: …the biggest fraud since Enron

scenes.narration: In court, the charitable image fell apart. The 'give it all away' story had been part of the sales pitch.
scenes.caption: …the halo was marketing

scenes.narration: The celebrities who'd advertised FTX got sued. The investors who'd skipped their homework lost billions.
scenes.caption: everyone who vouched for it paid

scenes.narration: And the real victims — millions of ordinary users — were left fighting for scraps in bankruptcy court.
scenes.caption: …ordinary users left in the cold

scenes.narration: At trial, the lifestyle came out. A thirty-million-dollar penthouse. Private jets. All quietly funded by customer deposits.
scenes.caption: …paid for with your money

scenes.narration: His defense was that he was just a disorganized founder who made mistakes. The jury didn't buy it.
scenes.caption: "just a founder who messed up"?
scenes.label: THE DEFENSE

scenes.narration: Because the backdoor wasn't a mistake. Someone wrote that code on purpose.
scenes.caption: …the backdoor was deliberate

scenes.narration: Prosecutors argued he hadn't lost track of the money. He'd stolen it — one deliberate line of code at a time.
Twenty-five years. From the cover of every magazine to a prison cell, in roughly a year.
scenes.caption: …magazine cover to prison cell

scenes.narration: His inner circle, who cooperated early, got far lighter sentences. In fraud, the first one to talk usually wins.
scenes.caption: …the first to flip wins

scenes.narration: So let's go back to the question. Where did the eight billion actually go?
Unlike Enron, this money was real — at first. It just got gambled and lost on bad bets and a lavish lifestyle.
scenes.caption: …gambled and lost

scenes.narration: The rest was a mirage. Billions in 'value' that only existed because of a coin FTX printed itself.
scenes.caption: …the rest was never real

scenes.narration: And here's the lesson that outlives FTX. On an exchange, the money in your account isn't really yours. It's an IOU.
scenes.caption: your balance is an IOU

scenes.narration: There's a saying in crypto. 'Not your keys, not your coins.' If someone else holds it, you're trusting them not to touch it.
scenes.caption: "not your keys, not your coins"

scenes.narration: The red flags were everywhere. No real board. No chief financial officer. Customer money mixed with the gambling fund.
scenes.caption: no board · no CFO · no limits

scenes.narration: But the charm covered it all. The hair, the beanbag, the promise to save the world — that was the real magic trick.
scenes.caption: charisma = the misdirection

scenes.narration: It made smart people, big investors, and regular users all stop asking one simple question. Where exactly is my money?
scenes.caption: …'where is my money?'

scenes.narration: Same as Enron, a new costume. Invent the value, hide the hole, and smile while everyone looks the other way.
scenes.caption: same trick, new costume

scenes.narration: There was no regulator checking FTX's books, because most of it sat offshore, beyond anyone's rules.
scenes.caption: …offshore, beyond the rules

scenes.narration: So the only thing standing between your savings and a trading desk was one man's word. And his word was worth nothing.
scenes.caption: …secured only by a promise

scenes.narration: The deepest lesson isn't about crypto at all. It's that trust, by itself, is not a safeguard.
scenes.caption: trust is not a safeguard

scenes.narration: Every giant fraud runs on the same fuel — a story good enough that people stop verifying it.
scenes.caption: …a story too good to check

scenes.narration: If you can't see where your money is held, assume someone else can spend it.
scenes.sub: …if you can't see it, be careful

scenes.narration: Not your keys, not your coins. Not your receipts, not your money. The form changes. The rule never does.
scenes.caption: verify. don't just trust.

scenes.narration: And to be fair, crypto wasn't the villain here. The technology didn't commit fraud. A person did.
scenes.caption: the tech didn't do this — a person did

scenes.narration: You can run the exact same scam with dollars, with stocks, with gold. FTX just did it faster, with fewer rules.
scenes.caption: …an old scam, new wrapper

scenes.narration: The pattern is always the same. A trusted face. A story too good to question. And money quietly moving where you can't see it.
scenes.caption: the eternal recipe for fraud

scenes.narration: So whenever something feels too safe, too generous, too good — that's exactly when to ask the boring question.
scenes.caption: "…where, exactly, is my money?"

scenes.narration: The eight billion dollars didn't vanish into the blockchain. It was gambled, spent, and lost — by people you were told to trust.
There is a simple fix, and crypto people love to repeat it. Hold your own money. Be your own bank.
scenes.caption: self-custody: hold your own keys

scenes.narration: But most people won't. It's hard, it's scary, and a friendly app is just so much easier to trust.
scenes.caption: …but trust is just easier

scenes.narration: Which is why this will happen again, in some new form, with some new charming face promising it's different.
scenes.caption: …so it'll happen again

scenes.narration: The names change — Enron, FTX, the next one. The trick is identical. Make the money invisible, and the story loud.
scenes.caption: same trick, new name

scenes.narration: The best protection isn't a law or an app. It's one stubborn habit. Follow the money until you can actually see it.
scenes.caption: follow it till you can SEE it

scenes.narration: So the next time an app shows you a glowing number and a famous face telling you it's safe — ask one boring question.
scenes.caption: ask the boring question

scenes.narration: Where is the actual money right now, and who can move it without asking me?
scenes.caption: where is it — and who holds the keys?

scenes.narration: If nobody can answer that in a sentence, you're not an investor. You're the collateral.
scenes.caption: …then you're the collateral

scenes.narration: Because in the end, a balance on a screen is just a promise. And a promise is only ever as good as the person making it.
scenes.caption: …a balance is just a promise

scenes.narration: If this made the smartest guys in crypto look a little less smart, hit subscribe — and tell me which collapse to break down next.
I do the reading. You get the parts that matter.

youtube.hook: In 2022, Sam Bankman-Fried was the most trusted man in crypto — FTX was worth $32 billion and he was the 'good billionaire' giving it all to charity. Then, in about 10 days, $8 billion of customer money vanished. The unsettling answer to where it went: it was secretly funneled to his trading firm Alameda through a backdoor in the code, propped up by a coin FTX printed itself. Here's exactly how it worked — fully cited.
